issues.legal_issue: The prosecution is not invariably required to examine every person who witnessed an occurrence, and omission of a witness is not necessarily fatal to the case.
material_facts: Four eyewitnesses testified about the assault, and the trial court and High Court found their evidence reliable and sufficient to support the convictions.
Other people said to have witnessed or arrived at the occurrence were not examined.
It was not shown that the unexamined witnesses were essential to complete the prosecution narrative or could speak to a matter on which the examined witnesses could not testify.
issues.conclusion: The failure to examine the other witnesses did not justify interfering with the convictions. The prosecution must examine witnesses essential to unfolding its case, and the court may draw an adverse inference if witnesses are withheld for improper reasons, including because their evidence would favour the accused.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution and the court share a duty to ensure that full and material facts are placed on the record to avoid miscarriage of justice. There is no absolute rule requiring every person present at an occurrence to testify: the effect of non-examination depends on the circumstances, including whether the witnesses examined provide reliable and sufficient evidence and whether an omitted witness is essential. A witness cannot properly be withheld merely because truthful evidence may favour the accused; where the reason for non-examination is untenable or improper, an adverse inference may be drawn. No earlier case or specific Evidence Act provision is cited in the judgment for this principle.

predicates.omitted_witnesses_not_shown_essential: The evidence does not show that the unexamined witnesses were essential to complete the case or to address a matter the testifying witnesses could not cover.

issues.definition: When a conviction appeal rests on reliable and sufficient eyewitness evidence and the omitted witnesses are not shown to be essential, their non-examination does not invalidate the prosecution case.

issues.legal_issue: Delay in recording an eyewitness's statement during the investigation does not by itself make the eyewitness's testimony unreliable.
material_facts: An eyewitness's name had been included in the first information report lodged within about three hours of the occurrence.
The eyewitness left the village the following morning to visit an ill relative, stayed away for several days, and the investigating officer recorded his statement after he returned.
Three other eyewitnesses had their statements recorded soon after the investigating officer reached the scene.
issues.conclusion: The delay in recording the eyewitness's statement did not justify rejecting his testimony, particularly in light of his prior identification in the first information report and the other eyewitness evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Whether delay in recording a witness's statement affects the reliability of the testimony depends on the circumstances. The court considered the witness's name being recorded in the prompt first information report, his absence from the village, and the supporting testimony of other eyewitnesses. No specific provision or earlier case is cited for this ruling.

issues.legal_issue: An omission from the first information report about the precise sequence of assaults is not material where the report otherwise describes the assault and the omission does not undermine the accused's liability.
material_facts: The first information report stated that the deceased was dragged and struck with the weapons.
The report did not expressly say that blows were inflicted before the deceased was dragged inside.
The eyewitnesses testified that blows were inflicted both before and after the deceased was dragged inside.
issues.conclusion: The omission did not make a material difference and did not exculpate any accused.
issues.legal_principle: An omission in an initial report is assessed in context; the omission of an express detail about the sequence of blows is not material where the report describes the dragging and blows and the omission does not affect the basis of liability. No specific provision or earlier case is cited for this ruling.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge that eyewitnesses are partisan does not warrant setting aside concurrent credibility findings when the courts have assessed the evidence and no cogent reason for a different view is shown.
material_facts: The appellants argued that the eyewitnesses were partisan and their testimony was unsafe to rely on.
The trial court and High Court considered the features of the case and found the eyewitnesses trustworthy and reliable.
No cogent ground was brought to the Supreme Court to justify taking a different view of the concurrent findings.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to reject the eyewitness evidence or interfere with the concurrent findings on the basis of the partisan-witness argument.
issues.legal_principle: A claim that witnesses are partisan must be considered in assessing their evidence, but it does not itself displace findings of credibility reached after consideration of the circumstances. In this appeal, the Court found no cogent ground to differ from the lower courts' assessment. No specific provision or earlier case is cited for this ruling.

issues.legal_issue: Where participants inflict a fatal assault in furtherance of their common object, the prosecution need not identify which participant caused each particular injury to sustain liability for the common-object offence.
material_facts: The accused were armed with heavy sharp-edged weapons, dragged the deceased inside a structure, and inflicted multiple blows on him.
The deceased suffered numerous injuries and died from injuries sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
The Court found that the injuries were inflicted in prosecution of the participants' common object to cause the deceased's death.
issues.conclusion: The inability of the witnesses to identify which accused inflicted each particular injury did not entitle the accused to relief.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied sections 148 and 302 read with section 149 of the Indian Penal Code. Where the fatal injuries are inflicted in prosecution of the participants' common object, the accused cannot obtain an advantage merely because the evidence does not assign each injury to a particular participant. No earlier case is cited for this ruling.
